issues.legal_issue: The statutory officer receiving a land-acquisition reference application cannot use the general power to excuse delay to extend the application deadline, even where a local amendment gives orders on such applications a limited route of judicial revision.
material_facts: The applicants were present when the land acquisition officer announced the award.
They applied for a reference after the applicable six-week period had expired.
The officer rejected the applications as time-barred.
The High Court treated the officer as a court for this purpose under a local amendment and condoned the delay, relying on the applicants’ efforts to obtain a copy of the award and consult counsel.
issues.conclusion: The officer was not a court for the purpose of extending the deadline, and the applications were barred by limitation. The officer had no power to extend the time for making them, so the High Court’s orders were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 18(1) and the proviso to Section 18(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, a timely written application is a condition for a valid reference; where the applicant was present or represented when the award was made, the application must be made within six weeks. The Collector acts as a statutory authority, distinct from the court defined in Section 3(d), and a local provision treating the Collector as a subordinate court for the limited purpose of revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not make the Collector a court for Section 5 of the Limitation Act. Section 5 applies to a court, while Section 29(2) does not supply an extension power in this setting. The Court relied on Mohd. Hasnuddin v. State of Maharashtra, which treated compliance with Section 18’s conditions, including limitation, as necessary for a valid reference; State of Punjab v. Satinder Bir Singh, which applied the statutory reference deadline; Nityananda, M. Joshi v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, Smt. Sushila Devi v. Ramanandan Prasad, and Mohd. Ashfaq v. State Transport Appellate Tribunal, concerning the limits of Section 5 when the decision-maker is not a court; and P.V. Gadgil v. P.Y. Deshpande, which rejected the same argument about the Collector’s status.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference_request and applicant_present_at_award and request_after_applicable_deadline and collector_acting_as_statutory_referrer

predicates.land_acquisition_reference_request: A person seeks a court’s determination of an objection to a land acquisition award by applying to the officer who received the objection.
predicates.applicant_present_at_award: The applicant was present or represented when the officer announced the award.
predicates.request_after_applicable_deadline: The applicant made the reference request after the deadline applicable to that applicant had expired.
predicates.collector_acting_as_statutory_referrer: The officer was performing the statutory function of deciding whether to refer the dispute to a court.

issues.definition: When an applicant who was present or represented at the award makes a land-acquisition reference request after its applicable deadline, and the officer is acting as the statutory referrer, the officer cannot extend that deadline.
